title: Data Architecture

toc.title: Business Drivers — 5 Roles of Data Architects
Cultural Factors for Adopting DA Practices (6)

html:
1Core Definition and Goals

Definition: Identifying the data needs of the enterprise (regardless of structure), and designing and maintaining the master blueprints to meet those needs. Using master blueprints to guide data integration, control data assets, and align data investments with business strategy.

ISO/IEC 42010:2007 definition of architecture: "The fundamental organization of a system, embodied in its components, their relationships to each other and the environment, and the principles governing its design and evolution."

Key concept: Architecture can refer to current state, future/proposed state, the discipline itself, the artifacts, or the team.

3 Goals of Data Architecture

  1. Identify data storage and processing requirements
  2. Design structures and plans to meet current and long-term data requirements of the enterprise
  3. Strategically prepare organizations to quickly evolve their products, services, and data to take advantage of business opportunities in emerging technologies

2Business Drivers — 5 Roles of Data Architects

Data Architecture bridges business strategy and technology execution. Data Architects:

  1. Strategically prepare organizations to quickly evolve products, services, and data for emerging technologies
  2. Translate business needs into data and system requirements so processes consistently have the data they need
  3. Manage complex data and information delivery throughout the enterprise
  4. Facilitate alignment between Business and IT
  5. Act as agents for change, transformation, and agility

34 Enterprise Architecture Domains

Data Architecture does not operate in isolation — it is one of four EA domains:

Domain Purpose Key Elements Roles
Enterprise Business Architecture How enterprise creates value for customers/stakeholders Business models, processes, capabilities, services, events, strategies, vocabulary Business architects, analysts, business data stewards
Enterprise Data Architecture How data should be organized and managed Data models, data definitions, data mapping specifications, data flows, structured data APIs Data architects, modelers, data stewards
Enterprise Applications Architecture Structure and functionality of applications Business systems, software packages, databases Applications architects
Enterprise Technology Architecture Physical technology to enable systems to function and deliver value Technical platforms, networks, security, integration tools Infrastructure architects

Dependency chain: Business Architecture establishes requirements → Data Architecture manages data created/required by BA → Application Architecture acts on data per business requirements → Technology Architecture hosts and executes application architecture.

4Enterprise Architecture Frameworks

An architecture framework is a foundational structure used to develop a broad range of related architectures — an "architecture for architecture."

IEEE Standard: ISO/IEC/IEEE 42010:2011 — Systems and Software Engineering — Architecture Description

Zachman Framework (Most Important)

  • Developed by John A. Zachman in the 1980s; most well-known enterprise architectural framework
  • An ontology — the 6×6 matrix comprises the complete set of models required to describe an enterprise and relationships between them
  • Does NOT define how to create models — it shows what models should exist
  • Each cell = a unique type of design artifact (intersection of row and column)

6 Columns — Communication Interrogatives

Column Question Represents
What Inventory column Entities used to build the architecture
How Process column Activities performed
Where Distribution column Business location and technology location
Who Responsibility column Roles and organizations
When Timing column Intervals, events, cycles, and schedules
Why Motivation column Goals, strategies, and means

6 Rows — Reification Transformations (Perspectives)

Row Perspective Role Focus
Row 1 Executive Planner (Identification) Business context, scope
Row 2 Business Management Owner (Definition) Business concepts, relationships
Row 3 Architect Designer (Representation) System logic, unconstrained design
Row 4 Engineer Builder (Specification) Technology physics, implementation
Row 5 Technician Implementer (Configuration) Component assemblies
Row 6 User Participant (Instantiation) Operational instances — no models

Reification = translating an abstract idea into a concrete instance.

5Enterprise Data Architecture (EDA)

Enterprise Data Architecture defines standard terms and designs for the elements important to the organization. It describes the collection, storage, integration, movement, and distribution of data.

EDA must include both:

Enterprise Data Model (EDM)

  • Holistic, enterprise-level, implementation-independent conceptual or logical data model
  • Provides a common, consistent view of data across the enterprise
  • Includes: key enterprise data entities (business concepts), their relationships, critical business rules, some critical attributes
  • Foundation for all data and data-related projects — any project-level model must be based on the EDM
  • Built incrementally and iteratively, using layers
  • Reviewed by stakeholders to achieve consensus

EDM Structure (4 levels of abstraction)

Level Description Scale
Conceptual Model 1 diagram of enterprise subject areas 12–20 significant subject areas with relationships
Subject Area Model 1+ diagram per subject area 50+ significant entities within subject area with relationships
Logical Model Detailed, partially attributed views per subject area Adds attributes and less-significant entities
Application/Project Models LDM + PDM specific to application or project Scoped to the subject and physical objects

EDM Linkages

  • Vertical: Models in each level map to models in other levels (creates model lineage)
  • Horizontal: Entities may appear in multiple models at the same level (external links between subject areas)

EDM Building Approaches

  • Top-down: Form Subject Areas first, then populate with models
  • Bottom-up: Subject Area structure based on existing data models
  • Combined (recommended): Start bottom-up with existing models, then complete by delegating Subject Area modeling to projects

Subject Area Discriminator Principles

  • Normalization rules (most effective for Data Architecture work)
  • Division from systems portfolios (funding)
  • Data governance structure and ownership (organizational)
  • Top-level business processes (value chains)
  • Business capabilities (EA-based)

Data Flow Design

  • A type of data lineage documentation that depicts how data moves through business processes and systems
  • End-to-end data flows illustrate: where data originated, where stored/used, how transformed
  • Maps data to:
    • Applications within a business process
    • Data stores or databases
    • Network segments (useful for security mapping)
    • Business roles (CRUD responsibilities)
    • Locations where local differences occur
  • Documented at different levels: Subject Area, business entity, or attribute level
  • Represented by: 2D matrices OR data flow diagrams
  • History: Matrix practice introduced by IBM (Business Systems Planning/BSP), later popularized by James Martin (Information Systems Planning/ISP) in the 1980s

6Activities

Activity 2.1: Establish Data Architecture Practice

Enterprise Data Architecture work streams (5):

  1. Strategy — Select frameworks, state approaches, develop roadmap
  2. Acceptance and culture — Inform and motivate changes in behavior
  3. Organization — Assign accountabilities and responsibilities
  4. Working methods — Define best practices within development projects, in coordination with EA
  5. Results — Produce Data Architecture artifacts within an overall roadmap

Activity 2.1.1: Evaluate Existing Data Architecture Specifications

Identify, evaluate for accuracy/completeness/detail, and update existing system documentation.

Activity 2.1.2: Develop a Roadmap

  • Describes the architecture's 3–5 year development path
  • Guided by a data management maturity assessment (see Chapter 15)
  • Must be integrated into the overall EA roadmap
  • Business-data-driven roadmap: starts with most independent business capabilities (least dependency) → ends with most dependent
  • Most independent capabilities = Master Data (Product Management, Customer Management)

Activity 2.1.3: Manage Enterprise Requirements within Projects

Data architects determine (at project completion):

  • Whether enterprise-wide entities conform to agreed standards
  • What entities should be included in overall EDA
  • Whether entities/definitions need generalization for future trends
  • Whether new data delivery architectures are indicated or whether to point to reuse

Implementation approach per methodology:

Method Approach
Waterfall Sequential phases, tollgates, include enterprise perspective
Incremental Mini-waterfalls, prototypes, comprehensive data design in early iterations
Agile/Iterative Sprints (Scrum, Rapid Dev, Unified Process); complete with data model specs for capture, storage, distribution

Activity 2.2: Integrate with Enterprise Architecture

Enterprise Data Architecture matters must be addressed proactively and integrated with project portfolio management.

7Tools

Tool Purpose
Data Modeling Tools Manage EDM at all levels; lineage and relation tracking between models
Asset Management Software Inventory systems, describe content, track relationships; collect Metadata about systems and data
Graphical Design Applications Create architectural design diagrams, data flows, data value chains, architectural artifacts

8Techniques

Lifecycle Projections — 8 Statuses

Status Meaning
Current Products currently supported and used
Deployment period Products deployed for use in next 1–2 years
Strategic period Products expected to be available in next 2+ years
Retirement Products retired or to be retired within a year
Preferred Products preferred for use by most applications
Containment Products limited to use by certain applications
Emerging Products being researched and piloted for possible future deployment
Reviewed Products evaluated; currently not in any other status

Diagramming Clarity — 6 Characteristics

  1. Clear and consistent legend — placed in same spot in all diagrams
  2. Match between diagram objects and legend — all diagram objects must match a legend object
  3. Clear and consistent line direction — flows start at one side, move toward opposite side
  4. Consistent line cross display — use line jumps; do not join lines to lines; minimize crossings
  5. Consistent object attributes — size/color/thickness differences must signify something
  6. Linear symmetry — objects placed in lines and columns; align at least half

9Implementation Guidelines

4 Components of DA Implementation:

  1. Organizing the Enterprise Data Architecture teams and forums
  2. Producing initial versions of DA artifacts (enterprise data model, enterprise-wide data flow, roadmaps)
  3. Forming and establishing a data architectural way of working in development projects
  4. Creating awareness throughout the organization of the value of Data Architecture

Traditional starting point: Master Data areas (greatest need for improvement) → expand to transactional data

10Implementation Risks (7)

  1. Lack of management support — new decision-makers may question/withdraw; enlist multiple senior management members
  2. No proven record of accomplishment — sponsor must have confidence; enlist senior architect colleague
  3. Apprehensive sponsor — sponsor requiring all communication through them; may be uncertain; must allow PM and architect to lead
  4. Counter-productive executive decisions — management understands value but not how to achieve it; need clearer/more frequent communication
  5. Culture shock — consider how working culture will change for affected employees
  6. Inexperienced project leader — ensure PM has experience with EDA for heavy data-component projects
  7. Dominance of a one-dimensional view — owners of one application (e.g., ERP) dictating overall architecture at expense of balanced enterprise view

11Cultural Factors for Adopting DA Practices (6)

  1. Cultural receptivity to architectural approach (architecture-friendly culture)
  2. Organizational recognition of data as a business asset, not just an IT concern
  3. Ability to let go of a local perspective and adopt an enterprise perspective on data
  4. Ability to integrate architectural deliverables into project methodology
  5. Level of acceptance of formal data governance
  6. Ability to look holistically at the enterprise (vs. focusing solely on project delivery and IT solutioning)

12Data Architecture Governance

Data Architects often act as business liaisons for data governance. EDA and DG organization must be well aligned.

Ideally: a Data Architect AND a Data Steward assigned to each subject area.

4 DG Activities in Data Architecture:

  1. Overseeing Projects — ensure projects comply with required DA activities, use/improve architectural assets, implement per standards
  2. Managing architectural designs, lifecycle, and tools — EDA serves as a 'zoning plan' for long-term integration; future state affects project priorities
  3. Defining standards — rules, guidelines, specifications for how data is used
  4. Creating data-related artifacts — artifacts that enable compliance with governance directives

13Metrics — 3 Categories

Architecture Standard Compliance Rate

  • Measures how closely projects comply with established Data Architectures
  • Tracks project exceptions as obstacles to adoption

Implementation Trends

  • Use/reuse/replace/retire measurements — proportion of new vs. reused/replaced/retired artifacts
  • Project execution efficiency — lead times, resource costs for delivery improvements

Business Value Measurements

  • Business agility improvements — lifecycle improvements or cost of delay
  • Business quality — whether business cases are fulfilled as intended
  • Business operation quality — improved efficiency; reduced time/expense correcting data errors
  • Business environment improvements — improved client retention, reduced regulatory remarks

14Context Diagram Summary

Component Key Items
Inputs Enterprise Architecture, Business Architecture, IT Standards and Goals, Data Strategies
Deliverables Data Architecture Design, Data Flows, Data Value Chains, Enterprise Data Model, Implementation Roadmap
Participants Enterprise Data Architects, Data Modelers
Suppliers Enterprise Architects, Data Stewards, Subject Matter Experts, Data Analysts
Consumers Database Administrators, Software Developers, Project Managers, Support Teams
Metrics Architecture standards compliance rates, Trends in implementation, Business value metrics
Tools Data modeling tools, Asset management software, Graphical design applications
Techniques Lifecycle Reviews, Diagramming Clarity

15Exam Q&A (20 Questions)

Q1. How is Data Architecture defined in DMBOK2? A: Identifying the data needs of the enterprise (regardless of structure), and designing and maintaining the master blueprints to meet those needs. Using master blueprints to guide data integration, control data assets, and align data investments with business strategy.

Q2. What are the 3 goals of Data Architecture? A: (1) Identify data storage and processing requirements; (2) Design structures and plans to meet current and long-term data requirements; (3) Strategically prepare organizations to quickly evolve products, services, and data for emerging technologies.

Q3. What role does Data Architecture play between business and technology? A: Data Architecture is a bridge between business strategy and technology execution.

Q4. What are the 4 Enterprise Architecture domains? A: Enterprise Business Architecture, Enterprise Data Architecture, Enterprise Applications Architecture, Enterprise Technology Architecture.

Q5. Who developed the Zachman Framework and when? A: John A. Zachman in the 1980s.

Q6. What is the Zachman Framework and what is its defining characteristic? A: An ontology — a 6×6 matrix comprising the complete set of models required to describe an enterprise. It shows WHAT models should exist but does NOT define HOW to create them. Each cell represents a unique type of design artifact.

Q7. What are the 6 communication interrogative columns in the Zachman Framework? A: What (inventory), How (process), Where (distribution), Who (responsibility), When (timing), Why (motivation).

Q8. What are the 6 reification transformation rows in the Zachman Framework? A: Executive (planner), Business Management (owner), Architect (designer), Engineer (builder), Technician (implementer), User (participant — no models at this level).

Q9. What are the two types of specifications that make up Enterprise Data Architecture? A: (1) Enterprise Data Model (EDM) — holistic, enterprise-level, implementation-independent conceptual/logical data model; (2) Data Flow Design — defines requirements and master blueprint for storage and processing across databases, applications, platforms, and networks.

Q10. What are the 4 levels of abstraction in an Enterprise Data Model? A: (1) Conceptual Model (12–20 subject areas); (2) Subject Area Model (50+ entities per subject area); (3) Logical Model (detailed, attributed views); (4) Application/Project-specific LDM and PDM.

Q11. What is the difference between vertical and horizontal linkages in an EDM? A: Vertical linkages map models between levels (e.g., physical table → logical entity → subject area entity → conceptual entity) — creates model lineage. Horizontal linkages show entities that appear in multiple models at the same level.

Q12. Who introduced the practice of using matrices for data flows, and when? A: IBM introduced this practice in its Business Systems Planning (BSP) method. James Martin later popularized it in Information Systems Planning (ISP) in the 1980s.

Q13. What does a Data Architecture roadmap describe, and how long is its horizon? A: A 3–5 year development path describing how the target architecture will become reality. Must be integrated into overall EA roadmap. Guided by data management maturity assessment.

Q14. How should a business-data-driven roadmap be sequenced? A: Start with the most independent business capabilities (least dependencies) — typically Master Data (Product and Customer Management) — and proceed toward the most dependent capabilities.

Q15. What are the 8 lifecycle projection statuses in Data Architecture? A: Current, Deployment period (1–2 years), Strategic period (2+ years), Retirement, Preferred, Containment, Emerging, Reviewed.

Q16. What are the 5 work streams in an Enterprise Data Architecture practice? A: Strategy, Acceptance and culture, Organization, Working methods, Results.

Q17. What are the 4 governance activities in Data Architecture? A: (1) Overseeing Projects; (2) Managing architectural designs, lifecycle, and tools; (3) Defining standards; (4) Creating data-related artifacts.

Q18. What is the most significant risk in Data Architecture initiation projects? A: Lack of management support — new decision-makers may question the process; requires enlisting multiple senior management members who understand the benefits.

Q19. What are the 3 metric categories for Data Architecture, and what does each cover? A: (1) Architecture standard compliance rate — project compliance with DA standards; (2) Implementation trends — use/reuse/replace/retire rates and project execution efficiency; (3) Business value measurements — agility, quality, operational quality, and environment improvements.

Q20. What is the most effective subject area discriminator principle for an enterprise data model? A: Normalization rules — the normalization process establishes the major entities that carry/constitute each Subject Area.
